fields.definition: Sympathetic vibration of the non-speaking (duplex) string segments in a grand piano — the front and rear portions of each string beyond the agraffe and bridge — which are proportioned to sound harmonics of the struck note, adding high-partial brilliance and sustain to the tone.
fields.plain_english: In a grand piano, the short bits of string on each side of the played part can be tuned to ring along with the note. This adds a bright, shimmering top to the sound.
fields.purpose_function: It enriches a piano's timbre by letting extra string lengths resonate, reinforcing upper harmonics so the instrument sounds brighter and more sustained without any added striking force.
fields.practical_application: An engineer close-miking a grand hears duplex resonance as extra sparkle and ring after each note, and can mute the duplex segments with felt strips when a cleaner, drier tone is wanted.
common_mistakes: Confusing designed duplex resonance with stray sympathetic ringing from other undamped strings.
Treating it as unwanted noise to eliminate rather than a built-in part of the tone.
Assuming every piano has tuned duplex segments, when many uprights and budget grands do not.
scenario_contexts: Close-miking a concert grand and noticing extra high-frequency shimmer after each note.
Damping the rear duplex with felt to tame brightness for a pop session.
Comparing the tonal halo of a piano with duplex scaling against one without it.

sources: Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (piano chapter)
Reblitz, Piano Servicing, Tuning, and Rebuilding

fields.definition: Striking a cymbal at its outer edge, rather than the bow or bell, to produce the loudest and most explosive attack, with a broad, fast-building spread of high overtones and a full crash character.
fields.plain_english: Hitting a cymbal right on its outer rim. It gives the biggest, brightest crash and is the loudest way to strike it.
fields.purpose_function: It gives a drummer the fullest, most cutting cymbal accent by exciting the widest range of vibration modes, producing a bright, sustaining crash that marks climaxes and transitions.
fields.practical_application: When micing cymbals, engineers expect edge strikes to peak much hotter than bow strikes, so they set gain and limiting to survive the transient without clipping.
common_mistakes: Aiming a mic straight at the edge, where the strike moves the most air and can overload the capsule.
Confusing an edge strike (crash) with a bow strike (ride ping).
UNSAFE: Ignoring the very high peak SPL of close-miked edge strikes, risking hearing damage without protection.
scenario_contexts: A drummer crashing a ride on the edge for a chorus accent.
Setting cymbal mic gain to handle loud edge strikes during a rock take.
Identifying edge-strike crashes versus bell hits while editing drum tracks.

sources: Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (percussion chapter)

fields.definition: A faint mechanical click in a grand piano's action at let-off, produced when the jack escapes from under the hammer knuckle and releases the hammer to fly to the string; an incidental noise heard just before or with the note attack.
fields.plain_english: A tiny click inside a grand piano when the key's lever lets the hammer go. It happens right as the note starts.
fields.purpose_function: The escapement (let-off) exists so the hammer flies free and rebounds instead of jamming against the string; the click is a by-product of that release, not a designed sound.
fields.practical_application: Engineers close-miking a piano may capture escapement clicks as mechanical noise and reduce them through mic placement, while a technician can regulate the action to quiet an overly loud let-off.
common_mistakes: Mistaking a normal escapement click for a fault or buzz in the instrument.
Adjusting the wrong part instead of regulating let-off to reduce it.
Assuming it can be removed entirely, when some mechanical noise is inherent to the action.
scenario_contexts: Hearing faint clicks under quiet passages on a close-miked solo piano recording.
A technician regulating let-off to quiet a noisy action.
Editing mechanical clicks out of an exposed, intimate piano track.

sources: Reblitz, Piano Servicing, Tuning, and Rebuilding
Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (piano action)

fields.definition: The onset transient of a note initiated directly by the finger — plucking a string with the fingertip or nail, or depressing a key — typically rounder and less percussive than the attack from a pick, hammer, or bow.
fields.plain_english: The start of a note made with the finger instead of a pick. It is usually softer and warmer than a pick's sharp attack.
fields.purpose_function: It shapes the very start of a note's envelope, and its gentler transient gives fingerstyle playing a warmer, more vocal character than plectrum or struck attacks.
fields.practical_application: An engineer choosing mics and compression for fingerstyle guitar or bass works with a softer attack transient than for pick playing, setting attack times to preserve the natural onset.
common_mistakes: Setting compressor attack too fast and squashing the soft finger transient flat.
Assuming a finger attack has no transient worth protecting and over-boosting highs.
Confusing finger attack (the note onset) with finger noise (incidental string sounds).
scenario_contexts: Recording fingerstyle acoustic guitar and choosing a compressor that keeps the gentle attack.
Dialing bass tone for a fingered part versus a picked part.
Comparing the softer onset of fingered notes with slapped or picked ones.

fields.definition: Incidental, non-pitched sounds produced by a player's fingers contacting the strings or fingerboard — squeaks, scrapes, buzzes and position-shift noises — regarded as an artifact when unwanted in a recording.
fields.plain_english: Extra little sounds the fingers make moving on the strings, like squeaks and scrapes. They are often unwanted noise on a recording.
fields.purpose_function: It is not a designed feature but a natural by-product of playing; spotting it lets a technician decide whether it adds realism or should be reduced.
fields.practical_application: Engineers cut distracting finger noise with mic placement, EQ dips in the squeak range, or editing, while leaving enough to keep a natural, human feel.
common_mistakes: Over-editing until the track sounds lifeless and unnatural.
Confusing normal finger noise with a mechanical fault in the instrument.
Boosting presence EQ so far that finger noise turns harsh and obvious.
scenario_contexts: Cleaning up an exposed solo acoustic guitar track.
Choosing a string type that squeaks less for a session.
Deciding how much natural finger noise to keep for realism.

fields.definition: Setting a string into vibration by pulling it aside with the fingertip or nail and releasing it (fingerstyle), producing a rounder, warmer attack and different harmonic emphasis than a plectrum.
fields.plain_english: Playing a string by pulling it with a finger and letting go. It gives a rounder, warmer sound than a pick.
fields.purpose_function: It is the basic fingerstyle way to excite a string, giving the player direct control of dynamics and tone and a softer onset than a pick.
fields.practical_application: Engineers record finger-plucked bass or guitar with attention to its fuller low end and softer transient, adjusting compression to suit.
common_mistakes: Assuming a finger pluck and a pick stroke need identical processing.
Overlooking hand and string position, which strongly change plucked tone.
Confusing a finger pluck with slap technique.
scenario_contexts: Tracking a fingerstyle electric bass line.
Recording classical guitar plucked with the nails.
Blending plucked and picked passages within one performance.

sources: Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (plucked strings)

fields.definition: The sound produced when a fingertip slides along the length of a string, either as an intentional glissando between notes or as an incidental squeak during a position shift on a fretted instrument.
fields.plain_english: The sound of a finger sliding along a string. It can be done on purpose between notes, or happen by accident when the hand shifts.
fields.purpose_function: As a technique it connects notes with a smooth glissando; as an artifact it marks hand movement, and telling the two apart helps a technician keep musical slides and reduce accidental ones.
fields.practical_application: Engineers keep expressive slides but tame unwanted slide squeaks with EQ or editing, and may suggest flatwound strings to reduce them.
common_mistakes: Editing out musical slides along with the unwanted squeaks.
Confusing an intentional glissando with accidental position-shift noise.
Assuming any string slides the same, when flatwounds squeak far less.
scenario_contexts: An electric guitar solo using slides for expression.
Cleaning accidental shift squeaks from an acoustic take.
Choosing strings to reduce slide noise for a close-miked session.

fields.definition: A sharp, broadband percussive transient produced by snapping the thumb and middle finger together so the finger strikes the palm; used as a rhythmic sound source and recognizable by its brief, click-like envelope.
fields.plain_english: The quick, sharp sound made by snapping your fingers. It is a short click used to keep or add rhythm.
fields.purpose_function: It provides a natural, portable percussive accent, common in vocal and pop arrangements, with a very fast attack and almost no sustain.
fields.practical_application: Engineers record finger snaps up close and often layer several takes for a fuller sound, using fast transient handling to keep the crisp attack.
common_mistakes: Recording a single snap and expecting it to sound big without layering.
Using slow compressor attack that dulls the snap's sharp transient.
Placing the mic so close the snap overloads the input.
scenario_contexts: Layering finger snaps as a backbeat in a pop production.
Capturing snaps for a sample library.
Adding live snaps over a sparse verse.

fields.definition: The squeaking sound made when a finger slides across the ridges of a round-wound string, caused by friction between skin and the winding; a common and often unwanted artifact on close-miked guitar and bass.
fields.plain_english: The squeak you hear when a finger slides over a wound string. It comes from the skin rubbing on the string's ridges.
fields.purpose_function: It is not a designed sound but a natural by-product of finger movement on wound strings; recognizing it lets a technician decide whether to keep it for realism or reduce it.
fields.practical_application: Engineers reduce finger squeak with flatwound or coated strings, string lubricant, EQ dips, or editing, keeping just enough for a natural feel.
common_mistakes: Trying to remove every squeak and making the track sound unnatural.
Blaming the instrument for a normal playing artifact.
Boosting high EQ that makes the squeaks worse.
scenario_contexts: An exposed acoustic guitar intro with audible string squeaks.
Switching to coated strings to cut squeak for a session.
Editing squeaks out of position shifts on a bass track.
